questions.question: A neuron receives a stimulus that is too weak to trigger a full voltage change. Which property of an action potential explains why no smaller spike appears?
options: It is all-or-nothing
It gradually loses amplitude
It is carried only by calcium
It always remains at resting voltage
questions.explanation: An action potential occurs as a complete voltage event rather than a partial spike. Treating an action potential as a graded response ignores its all-or-nothing behavior.
questions.sourceEvidence: An action potential is a rapid, all-or-nothing change in a neuron’s membrane voltage.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating an action potential as a graded response ignores its all-or-nothing behavior

questions.question: Why can an action potential travel a long distance along an axon without becoming progressively smaller?
options: ATP molecules physically carry the voltage forward
Voltage-gated channels regenerate the membrane-voltage change
Neurotransmitters diffuse along the entire axon
The resting potential becomes increasingly positive
questions.explanation: Sequential voltage-gated channel activity restores the signal as it propagates. Assuming passive diffusion alone carries the signal predicts an amplitude loss that action potentials avoid.
questions.sourceEvidence: Voltage-gated ion channels first reverse and then restore the membrane potential, creating a signal that travels along the axon without losing amplitude.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming passive diffusion alone carries the signal predicts an amplitude loss that action potentials avoid

questions.question: What conversion occurs when an action potential reaches the axon terminal?
options: A chemical message becomes DNA
Mechanical energy becomes heat
An electrical signal becomes a chemical message
A protein gradient becomes an electrical signal
questions.explanation: Synaptic transmission changes the arriving electrical event into neurotransmitter signaling. Keeping the signal purely electrical overlooks the chemical step between cells.
questions.sourceEvidence: At the axon terminal, synaptic transmission converts the electrical signal into a chemical message that can influence another cell.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Keeping the signal purely electrical overlooks the chemical step between cells

questions.question: Which observation best identifies a recorded event as an action potential?
options: Every event has a size proportional to stimulus strength
The voltage never changes from rest
Only the cell body shows a voltage change
Every successful event has the same characteristic size
questions.explanation: All successful action potentials follow the all-or-nothing pattern. Confusing spike amplitude with stimulus intensity describes a graded potential rather than an action potential.
questions.sourceEvidence: An action potential is a rapid, all-or-nothing change in a neuron’s membrane voltage.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing spike amplitude with stimulus intensity describes a graded potential rather than an action potential

questions.question: A drug prevents voltage-gated ion channels from opening along an axon. What is the most direct consequence?
options: The action potential cannot propagate normally
The axon produces more neurotransmitter at rest
The membrane becomes a phospholipid monolayer
The nucleus begins translating proteins
questions.explanation: Propagation depends on voltage-gated channels reversing and restoring membrane voltage. Attributing axonal propagation to neurotransmitter diffusion places the chemical step in the wrong location.
questions.sourceEvidence: Voltage-gated ion channels first reverse and then restore the membrane potential, creating a signal that travels along the axon without losing amplitude.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Attributing axonal propagation to neurotransmitter diffusion places the chemical step in the wrong location

questions.question: How does activity in one neuron gain the ability to influence a neighboring cell?
options: The action potential crosses the synaptic gap unchanged
Synaptic transmission relays a chemical message at the terminal
The neighboring cell shares the same cytoplasm
The axon transfers its ion channels into the next cell
questions.explanation: The axon terminal initiates a chemical message that can act on another cell. Assuming the electrical spike directly jumps between ordinary neurons skips synaptic transmission.
questions.sourceEvidence: At the axon terminal, synaptic transmission converts the electrical signal into a chemical message that can influence another cell.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming the electrical spike directly jumps between ordinary neurons skips synaptic transmission

questions.question: Two electrodes placed far apart on the same healthy axon record propagated action potentials. What should they show?
options: A much smaller spike at the second electrode
A permanently positive membrane at the second electrode
Similar spike amplitudes at both locations
Chemical neurotransmitter release all along the axon
questions.explanation: Regenerative channel activity preserves action-potential amplitude along the axon. Expecting the spike to fade treats it like a passive voltage spread rather than a regenerated signal.
questions.sourceEvidence: Voltage-gated ion channels first reverse and then restore the membrane potential, creating a signal that travels along the axon without losing amplitude.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Expecting the spike to fade treats it like a passive voltage spread rather than a regenerated signal

questions.question: At a resting membrane potential of −70 mV, how is the inside of the neuron charged relative to the outside?
options: The inside is 70 mV more negative
The inside is 70 mV more positive
Both sides have identical charge
The outside contains no charged ions
questions.explanation: A negative membrane potential means the interior is negative relative to the exterior. Reading the minus sign as a positive interior reverses the voltage convention.
questions.sourceEvidence: The resting membrane potential of approximately −70 mV (inside negative relative to outside) exists because of two factors: the selective permeability of the membrane and the activity of the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reading the minus sign as a positive interior reverses the voltage convention

questions.question: Which ion has the greater resting permeability across the neuronal membrane?
options: Na⁺
K⁺
Ca²⁺
Cl⁻ only
questions.explanation: Open potassium leak channels make the resting membrane more permeable to K⁺ than Na⁺. Assuming all ions cross equally ignores selective membrane permeability.
questions.sourceEvidence: At rest, the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than Na⁺.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming all ions cross equally ignores selective membrane permeability

questions.question: Why does K⁺ leakage help make the neuronal interior negative?
options: Negative charge leaves while proteins move outside
K⁺ entry neutralizes every internal protein
Positive charge leaves while negative proteins remain inside
The pump converts K⁺ into electrons
questions.explanation: K⁺ efflux removes positive charge and leaves impermeant negative proteins behind. Claiming that K⁺ influx creates resting negativity reverses the leak direction.
questions.sourceEvidence: K⁺ ions leak out down their concentration gradient through open K⁺ leak channels, carrying positive charges out and leaving behind negatively charged proteins inside.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Claiming that K⁺ influx creates resting negativity reverses the leak direction

questions.question: One complete Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase cycle moves which combination of ions?
options: 2 Na⁺ out and 3 K⁺ in
3 Na⁺ in and 2 K⁺ out
Equal numbers of Na⁺ and K⁺ outward
3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in
questions.explanation: The pump exports three sodium ions while importing two potassium ions. Reversing the pump stoichiometry destroys the gradients it normally maintains.
questions.sourceEvidence: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump continuously restores the gradients — moving 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in — and contributes to the net negative interior.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reversing the pump stoichiometry destroys the gradients it normally maintains

questions.question: What is the net movement of positive charge during one Na⁺/K⁺ pump cycle?
options: One positive charge moves outward
One positive charge moves inward
Five positive charges move outward
There is no net charge movement
questions.explanation: Exporting three positive ions and importing two gives a net outward movement of one positive charge. Calling the pump electrically neutral ignores the unequal three-to-two exchange.
questions.sourceEvidence: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump continuously restores the gradients — moving 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in — and contributes to the net negative interior.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling the pump electrically neutral ignores the unequal three-to-two exchange

questions.question: Why is the resting potential useful even before a neuron fires?
options: It permanently locks every ion channel
It stores electrical potential energy
It synthesizes neurotransmitter from DNA
It removes all concentration gradients
questions.explanation: The separated charges across the membrane store energy that can drive a rapid signal. Describing rest as an inactive zero-energy state overlooks the stored electrochemical energy.
questions.sourceEvidence: This stored electrical potential is critical because it represents potential energy.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Describing rest as an inactive zero-energy state overlooks the stored electrochemical energy

questions.question: If ion permeability changes rapidly after stimulation, what can the neuron do with its resting potential?
options: Stop all ion movement permanently
Translate mRNA inside the membrane
Generate a fast signal along the axon
Turn the axon terminal into a nucleus
questions.explanation: Changes in permeability release stored electrical potential into a traveling signal. Treating permeability changes as unrelated to voltage misses the mechanism of electrical signaling.
questions.sourceEvidence: When a neuron is stimulated, rapid changes to ion permeability can use this potential energy to generate a fast electrical signal that travels the length of the axon.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating permeability changes as unrelated to voltage misses the mechanism of electrical signaling

questions.question: A stimulus raises a neuron from −70 mV to −60 mV and then stops. What is the expected response?
options: The membrane returns to rest without a full action potential
A full action potential must occur
The neuron remains permanently at −60 mV
The spike amplitude doubles
questions.explanation: A membrane voltage of −60 mV remains below the approximate −55 mV threshold. Assuming every depolarization triggers a spike ignores the threshold requirement.
questions.sourceEvidence: Below the threshold potential (approximately −55 mV), Na⁺ channels do not open sufficiently and the membrane returns to rest.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming every depolarization triggers a spike ignores the threshold requirement

questions.question: A second stimulus pushes the same neuron to −50 mV. What happens next?
options: Only a half-sized action potential occurs
Positive feedback produces a full action potential
All sodium channels remain closed
The membrane immediately settles at −80 mV
questions.explanation: Crossing −55 mV recruits self-amplifying Na⁺ entry and a complete spike. Making spike size proportional to the amount above threshold violates all-or-nothing signaling.
questions.sourceEvidence: Once threshold is reached, positive feedback takes over: Na⁺ entry depolarizes the membrane further, which opens more Na⁺ channels, which allows more Na⁺ in — creating a self-amplifying cascade that always produces the same magnitude signal regardless of how much above threshold the original stimulus was.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Making spike size proportional to the amount above threshold violates all-or-nothing signaling

questions.question: What creates positive feedback during the rising phase of an action potential?
options: K⁺ entry closes every sodium channel
ATP directly raises the membrane voltage
Na⁺ entry opens still more voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Neurotransmitter leaves through leak channels
questions.explanation: Incoming Na⁺ depolarizes the membrane and recruits additional Na⁺ channels. Attributing the rising phase to K⁺ efflux reverses the relevant ion movement.
questions.sourceEvidence: Once threshold is reached, positive feedback takes over: Na⁺ entry depolarizes the membrane further, which opens more Na⁺ channels, which allows more Na⁺ in — creating a self-amplifying cascade that always produces the same magnitude signal regardless of how much above threshold the original stimulus was.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Attributing the rising phase to K⁺ efflux reverses the relevant ion movement

questions.question: How does a neuron usually represent a stronger stimulus?
options: It makes each action potential taller
It changes every spike into a graded potential
It lowers the number of spikes to zero
It fires action potentials more frequently
questions.explanation: Stimulus intensity is encoded by firing frequency rather than individual spike size. Using amplitude as the intensity code contradicts the fixed magnitude of action potentials.
questions.sourceEvidence: Signal strength is therefore not encoded in the size of individual action potentials but in their frequency.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Using amplitude as the intensity code contradicts the fixed magnitude of action potentials

questions.question: A sensory neuron changes from 5 spikes per second to 50 spikes per second. What has most likely changed?
options: The encoded stimulus intensity has increased
Each spike now travels backward
The resting potential has become zero
The neuron has lost all voltage-gated channels
questions.explanation: A higher action-potential frequency is interpreted as a stronger stimulus. Interpreting the change as larger individual spikes confuses frequency with amplitude.
questions.sourceEvidence: A weak stimulus might cause 5 action potentials per second; a stronger stimulus causes 50.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Interpreting the change as larger individual spikes confuses frequency with amplitude

questions.question: What does rate coding mean in neuronal signaling?
options: Information is carried only by axon diameter
Information about intensity is carried by spike frequency
Every stimulus changes the spike amplitude
Only inhibitory signals can encode intensity
questions.explanation: Rate coding uses the number of action potentials per unit time as an intensity signal. Defining rate coding by spike height mistakes amplitude for firing rate.
questions.sourceEvidence: The nervous system interprets frequency as intensity — a code called rate coding.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Defining rate coding by spike height mistakes amplitude for firing rate

questions.question: Why do voltage-gated Na⁺ channels give the action potential an all-or-nothing character?
options: They continuously leak at the same rate
They release neurotransmitter directly into the nucleus
Their threshold-dependent opening recruits a complete regenerative response
They keep membrane voltage fixed at −70 mV
questions.explanation: Threshold activation of Na⁺ channels initiates the self-amplifying depolarization. Calling the response gradual ignores the regenerative recruitment of sodium channels.
questions.sourceEvidence: An action potential is all-or-nothing because of the voltage-gated Na⁺ channels involved.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling the response gradual ignores the regenerative recruitment of sodium channels

questions.question: Which channel changes initiate repolarization near the peak of an action potential?
options: Na⁺ channels inactivate while voltage-gated K⁺ channels open
Na⁺ channels open while K⁺ channels close
Both ion types stop moving permanently
Ca²⁺ channels replace every potassium channel
questions.explanation: Sodium-channel inactivation ends inward current while potassium channels create outward current. Reversing the channel states would continue depolarization instead of repolarizing the membrane.
questions.sourceEvidence: Near the action-potential peak, Na⁺ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reversing the channel states would continue depolarization instead of repolarizing the membrane

questions.question: What ion movement directly drives the membrane back toward a negative voltage?
options: Na⁺ enters the neuron
K⁺ leaves the neuron
K⁺ enters the neuron
Proteins leave through sodium channels
questions.explanation: Outward movement of positive K⁺ charge makes the interior more negative again. Assigning repolarization to Na⁺ influx confuses the falling phase with depolarization.
questions.sourceEvidence: K⁺ flows out, returning the membrane toward a negative voltage.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assigning repolarization to Na⁺ influx confuses the falling phase with depolarization

questions.question: Why does membrane voltage briefly reach about −80 mV after a spike?
options: Na⁺ channels remain fully open
All ions reach equal concentrations
Voltage-gated K⁺ channels close slowly
The membrane loses every leak channel
questions.explanation: Continued K⁺ efflux after rest is crossed produces temporary hyperpolarization. Blaming hyperpolarization on prolonged Na⁺ entry predicts movement in the wrong voltage direction.
questions.sourceEvidence: Because K⁺ channels close slowly, the potential briefly falls below rest to about −80 mV, a phase called hyperpolarization, before leak channels and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump restore resting conditions.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Blaming hyperpolarization on prolonged Na⁺ entry predicts movement in the wrong voltage direction

questions.question: Can any stimulus trigger a second action potential during the absolute refractory period?
options: Yes, if the stimulus is twice as strong
Yes, because K⁺ channels create another rising phase
No, because all ATP has been consumed
No, inactivated Na⁺ channels cannot reopen yet
questions.explanation: Sodium-channel inactivation prevents another spike regardless of stimulus strength. Treating the absolute period like the relative period incorrectly makes it surmountable.
questions.sourceEvidence: During the absolute refractory period, inactivated Na⁺ channels cannot reopen, so another action potential cannot begin.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating the absolute period like the relative period incorrectly makes it surmountable

questions.question: Why might a very strong stimulus trigger a spike during the relative refractory period when a weak one cannot?
options: The hyperpolarized membrane is farther from threshold
Every Na⁺ channel has been permanently removed
The resting voltage is already above threshold
Neurotransmitters cannot bind during this period
questions.explanation: Hyperpolarization increases the depolarization needed to reach threshold. Claiming no stimulus can work confuses the relative refractory period with the absolute period.
questions.sourceEvidence: The relative refractory period during hyperpolarization requires a stronger stimulus.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Claiming no stimulus can work confuses the relative refractory period with the absolute period

questions.question: How do refractory periods support one-way propagation along an axon?
options: They make the next axon segment permanently inactive
The membrane just behind the spike cannot immediately fire again
They force neurotransmitter to flow through the axon
They increase spike amplitude toward the cell body
questions.explanation: Recently activated membrane is refractory while the membrane ahead remains excitable. Assuming both directions are equally excitable ignores the temporary inactivation behind the wave.
questions.sourceEvidence: These periods limit firing frequency and ensure that propagation moves forward rather than backward.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming both directions are equally excitable ignores the temporary inactivation behind the wave

questions.question: What sets an upper limit on how rapidly a neuron can fire repeated action potentials?
options: The height of each action potential
The number of ribosomes in the axon
The time required to pass through refractory periods
The width of the synaptic cleft alone
questions.explanation: Absolute and relative refractory periods restrict how soon another spike can occur. Attributing the firing limit to spike amplitude ignores channel recovery time.
questions.sourceEvidence: These periods limit firing frequency and ensure that propagation moves forward rather than backward.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Attributing the firing limit to spike amplitude ignores channel recovery time

questions.question: What is the first channel event at an axon terminal after an action potential arrives?
options: Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open
Voltage-gated K⁺ channels release neurotransmitter
Aquaporins pump sodium outward
Postsynaptic receptors enter the nucleus
questions.explanation: Terminal depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels. Starting with vesicle fusion before calcium entry reverses the causal sequence.
questions.sourceEvidence: When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, it triggers voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels to open.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Starting with vesicle fusion before calcium entry reverses the causal sequence

questions.question: How does Ca²⁺ entry lead to neurotransmitter release?
options: It carries neurotransmitter through potassium channels
It triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane
It converts neurotransmitter into ATP
It closes the synaptic cleft
questions.explanation: Calcium stimulates vesicle fusion and exocytosis at the presynaptic terminal. Treating calcium itself as the neurotransmitter cargo confuses trigger with message.
questions.sourceEvidence: Calcium ions flood into the terminal, causing synaptic vesicles (membrane-bound packages of neurotransmitter) to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their neurotransmitter molecules into the synaptic cleft by exocytosis.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating calcium itself as the neurotransmitter cargo confuses trigger with message

questions.question: After exocytosis, where do neurotransmitter molecules bind?
options: Ribosomes inside the presynaptic nucleus
Leak channels along the myelin sheath
Receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
ATP synthase in the mitochondrial matrix
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitters cross the cleft and bind receptors on the receiving cell. Placing the receptors on the presynaptic release membrane reverses sender and receiver.
questions.sourceEvidence: The neurotransmitters diffuse across the narrow cleft (20–40 nm) and bind to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Placing the receptors on the presynaptic release membrane reverses sender and receiver

questions.question: What opposite effects do EPSPs and IPSPs have on a postsynaptic neuron?
options: Both always trigger an action potential
EPSPs move it away while IPSPs move it toward threshold
Both permanently block sodium channels
EPSPs move it toward threshold while IPSPs move it away
questions.explanation: Excitatory potentials favor threshold while inhibitory potentials oppose it. Swapping EPSP and IPSP effects reverses excitation and inhibition.
questions.sourceEvidence: Whether the postsynaptic neuron fires depends on summation: excitatory inputs (EPSPs) bring the membrane toward threshold; inhibitory inputs (IPSPs) move it away.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Swapping EPSP and IPSP effects reverses excitation and inhibition

questions.question: Several different presynaptic neurons fire at the same moment. What process combines their effects?
options: Spatial summation
Temporal summation
Saltatory conduction
Hyperpolarization only
questions.explanation: Spatial summation integrates inputs arriving simultaneously from multiple synapses. Calling this temporal summation ignores that the inputs come from different synapses.
questions.sourceEvidence: The postsynaptic neuron integrates all incoming signals simultaneously — spatial summation (multiple synapses firing at once) and temporal summation (repeated signals from one synapse in quick succession) — and fires only if the net effect reaches threshold.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling this temporal summation ignores that the inputs come from different synapses

questions.question: One presynaptic neuron fires repeatedly in rapid succession. What process can add those inputs together?
options: Spatial summation
Temporal summation
Osmosis
Absolute refractoriness
questions.explanation: Temporal summation combines closely spaced signals from one synapse. Calling this spatial summation ignores the repeated timing at a single synapse.
questions.sourceEvidence: The postsynaptic neuron integrates all incoming signals simultaneously — spatial summation (multiple synapses firing at once) and temporal summation (repeated signals from one synapse in quick succession) — and fires only if the net effect reaches threshold.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Calling this spatial summation ignores the repeated timing at a single synapse

questions.question: Which sign correctly describes the inside of a resting neuron?
options: Negative at about −70 mV relative to outside
Positive at about +70 mV relative to outside
Exactly 0 mV at all times
Positive only because K⁺ is present
questions.explanation: The resting voltage is negative inside relative to the extracellular side. Dropping the minus sign reverses the polarity of the resting membrane.
questions.sourceEvidence: The resting potential is about −70 mV inside, not positive.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Dropping the minus sign reverses the polarity of the resting membrane

questions.question: Which ion distribution is typical before an action potential?
options: High Na⁺ inside and high K⁺ outside
High K⁺ inside and high Na⁺ outside
Equal Na⁺ and K⁺ on both sides
No K⁺ inside and no Na⁺ outside
questions.explanation: Resting neurons maintain potassium-rich cytoplasm and sodium-rich extracellular fluid. Reversing the gradients predicts the wrong directions for depolarizing and repolarizing currents.
questions.sourceEvidence: K⁺ concentration is high inside and Na⁺ concentration is high outside.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reversing the gradients predicts the wrong directions for depolarizing and repolarizing currents

questions.question: A membrane changes from −70 mV to −60 mV. How should this change be described?
options: Repolarization because the interior is more negative
Hyperpolarization because the voltage is closer to zero
Depolarization because the interior is less negative
No voltage change because both values are negative
questions.explanation: Moving toward zero from a negative resting value is depolarization. Assuming depolarization must make the inside positive overlooks subthreshold voltage changes.
questions.sourceEvidence: Depolarization means the interior becomes less negative.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming depolarization must make the inside positive overlooks subthreshold voltage changes

questions.question: A stronger stimulus reaches a neuron that is already above threshold. What feature of its output normally increases?
options: Action-potential amplitude
Resting-potential sign
Width of the synaptic cleft
Action-potential frequency
questions.explanation: Stronger stimuli are encoded by more frequent fixed-size spikes. Making each spike taller violates the all-or-nothing principle.
questions.sourceEvidence: Once threshold is crossed, action potentials are all-or-nothing; stronger stimuli increase frequency, not amplitude.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Making each spike taller violates the all-or-nothing principle

questions.question: How does myelin increase conduction speed?
options: It supports saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier
It releases neurotransmitter along every internode
It removes all refractory periods
It makes action potentials larger at each node
questions.explanation: Myelin allows excitation to advance efficiently from node to node. Describing myelin as a neurotransmitter source confuses insulation with synaptic release.
questions.sourceEvidence: Myelin speeds conduction through saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Describing myelin as a neurotransmitter source confuses insulation with synaptic release

questions.question: Which description correctly assigns the direction of chemical synaptic signaling?
options: Neurotransmitter leaves the postsynaptic cell and binds the presynaptic cell
Neurotransmitter leaves the presynaptic cell and binds the postsynaptic cell
The action potential carries receptors across the cleft
The two cells exchange their membranes
questions.explanation: The presynaptic terminal releases the signal and the postsynaptic membrane receives it. Reversing pre and postsynaptic roles swaps the sender with the receiver.
questions.sourceEvidence: Neurotransmitters leave the presynaptic cell and bind receptors on the postsynaptic cell.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reversing pre and postsynaptic roles swaps the sender with the receiver
